Sequre is placed in that survey as a Python-like DSL compiling through a custom intermediate form before lowering to LLVM and native code -- a characterisation of the Codon path, arrived at without naming Codon. The pipeline itself is separate work.
entries.why_codon: The related-work section describes Sequre's compilation path and positions the paper's own IR against it. No Codon or Sequre code is run.
entries.note: Illustrates a pattern in the Sequre-only citation group: the MPC literature engages with Sequre's compiler design while treating Codon underneath it as an implementation detail, so these citations reach Codon at one remove.

entries.name: Streamlining C Compilation: Harnessing Different Optimization Techniques
entries.summary: A review of compiler optimisation techniques, working through recent papers one by one and stating what each contributes and where it falls short. Codon is one of those, credited with reaching C and C++ performance from Python while remaining domain-extensible, and then held to the two limitations the Codon paper names for itself.
entries.why_codon: The review summarises Codon as a domain-extensible compiler achieving low-level performance from Python syntax, and then states that support for runtime polymorphism and standard library coverage remain limited. Nothing is run.
entries.note: One of the few citations that repeats Codon's stated limitations rather than only its results. Runtime polymorphism is the one it names first, and it is also exactly what Pyls exists to supply for Python hardware synthesis -- the same gap read as a caveat here and as an opportunity there.

entries.name: Anonify: Decentralized Dual-level Anonymity for Medical Data Donation
entries.summary: A scheme giving medical data donors anonymity both from the recipient and from each other, set against the trade-off between privacy and utility that k-anonymity and differential privacy each force. Sequre is one of three citations supporting the sentence that many data-sharing protocols build on secure multiparty computation.
entries.why_codon: Sequre is cited once, bracketed alongside two other works in a list of secure multiparty computation protocols. Nothing is run.

entries.name: Genomic privacy preservation in genome-wide association studies: taxonomy, limitations, challenges, and vision
entries.summary: A taxonomy of privacy-preserving methods for genome-wide association studies, tabulating each published approach by the privacy technique it uses and the statistical test it supports. Sequre occupies one row of that table, recorded as a secure multiparty computation protocol covering GWAS, drug-target interaction prediction and metagenomic binning.
entries.why_codon: Sequre is catalogued in the survey's table of secure multiparty computation approaches and described in one sentence of the accompanying prose. The survey classifies published work and runs none of it.
entries.note: First work in the corpus filed with provenance `survey`. It also carries the SECRET-GWAS preprint DOI in its bibliography, which is what made the local ingest report it as two candidates before the identifier learned to prefer a DOI printed before the references heading.

entries.name: JACC: Leveraging HPC Meta-Programming and Performance Portability with the Just-in-Time and LLVM-based Julia Language
entries.summary: A portability layer for Julia that keeps one source form across CPU and GPU back ends, set against the wider movement of high-level languages onto LLVM. Codon is named alongside Numba as an effort targeting Python that reuses LLVM's modularity by generating LLVM IR.
entries.why_codon: Codon is cited once, bracketed with Numba, as an effort targeting Python that generates LLVM IR to get performance from a high-level dynamic programming model. No experiment involves it.
entries.note: Another citation that reaches for the intermediate representation rather than the benchmark numbers, consistent with the split this corpus keeps showing between compiler-facing and application-facing readers.

entries.name: SECRET-GWAS: Confidential Computing for Population-Scale GWAS
entries.summary: A genome-wide association study framework built on trusted execution rather than secret sharing, reporting four million SNPs over one million patients on 1,024 cores in 29 minutes. Sequre is the comparison point it argues against: the paper quotes Sequre's own published estimate of three weeks for a comparable linear-regression pipeline and positions its measured runtime against that figure.
entries.why_codon: The paper describes Sequre as a framework for quick development of MPC programs and quotes its published runtime estimate for a full GWAS pipeline. The comparison is against that stated figure; Sequre is not built or run here.
entries.note: The closest any citation in the corpus has come to `evaluates` while remaining `prior_art`. A comparison is genuinely published, but against a number quoted from Sequre's paper rather than a run the authors performed, and ruling 7 draws the line at whether Codon executed. Worth his eye if the distinction should be recorded differently.

entries.name: IR Design for Application-Specific Natural Language: A Case Study on Traffic Data
entries.summary: An intermediate representation for a natural-language interface over traffic data, surveying MLIR and LLVM as the general-purpose optimisation frameworks it positions itself against. Codon is cited once, and the sentence it supports is about LLVM IR rather than about Codon.
entries.why_codon: The single citation attaches to the claim that LLVM implements its code optimisation through LLVM IR. Codon is the reference given for that general statement about LLVM, and nothing about Codon itself is described or run.
entries.note: The second miscitation found in the corpus, after the genomic inference survey cited Sequre for homomorphic encryption. Both are recorded as they stand, because how a work is cited is what an index of reception should show. Note also that this work is one Semantic Scholar holds and OpenAlex does not, which is the recall gap the paper lane was set up to expose.

entries.name: COLLAGENE enables privacy-aware federated and collaborative genomic data analysis
entries.summary: A toolbase for collaborative genomic analysis across sites that will not pool their data, built on homomorphic encryption and deliberately usable from ordinary shell and R workflows. Sequre appears twice in the survey of alternatives and once as a row in the paper's table of existing tools, and both prose mentions turn on the same objection: that approaches built on a specialised programming language ask more of their users.
entries.why_codon: Sequre is described as an MPC pipeline-building effort that can benefit more advanced users because it uses a specialised programming language, and later as a library using a modified programming language which can optimise low-level implementations at the expense of complexity and maintainability. It is tabulated but never run.
entries.note: The first citation in the corpus that argues against the approach rather than merely reporting it, and it appears in Genome Biology, the venue that published Sequre. The cost it names -- complexity and maintainability -- is the cost of the compiler bet itself, so it is the sharpest external appraisal the index holds.

entries.name: D2X: An eXtensible conteXtual Debugger for Modern DSLs
entries.summary: A debugger that carries domain-specific state out of a DSL compiler and into the debugging session, on the argument that ordinary source-level debuggers show the generated code without the compiler's own inferred information. Seq is the motivating example of that problem: a dynamically typed genomics DSL whose statically inferred types exist in neither the source nor the binary.
entries.why_codon: Seq appears exactly once in the body, as the example of a DSL whose inferred type information is hidden inside the compiler. The paper's two case studies are GraphIt and BuildIt; Seq is not instrumented and not run.
entries.note: Published at the same venue that would publish Codon the same year. The citation is unusual in being about what a Codon-family compiler KNOWS rather than how fast it is -- type information the compiler infers and then discards from view. Recovered through DSpace@MIT after the ACM Digital Library served a bot challenge, the third time an institutional repository has been the route to an MIT-authored closed paper.

entries.name: Detecting Interpreter Bugs via Filling Function Calls in Skeletal Program Enumeration
entries.summary: FCFuzzer extends skeletal program enumeration by filling in function calls, and is turned on seven Python implementations at once: CPython, IronPython, GPython, Pyston, PyPy, RustPython and Codon v0.15.5. A month of fuzzing produced 35 interpreter bugs, 16 of them previously unknown, and Codon is among the implementations that crashed.
entries.why_codon: Codon is one of the seven Python implementations under test, named with the version used and appearing in the results table with reported crashes. The paper runs it as a subject of the study rather than citing it.
entries.note: The only work in the corpus that treats Codon as a program under test rather than a tool or a citation, and the only one to file bugs against it. It also sets Codon among Python interpreters rather than among compilers, which is a category error the paper's own description avoids -- and one that makes Codon look worse, since a compiler that rejects a dynamic program is behaving as designed. Two Codon crashes appear in the table, one recorded as already known upstream.

entries.name: nelli: a lightweight frontend for MLIR
entries.summary: A Python frontend for MLIR that leans on Python's own lexer and AST machinery rather than rebuilding a compiler frontend. Codon is one of three citations for the observation that building such a frontend for numerics-intensive Python has been attempted many times with varying success.
entries.why_codon: Codon is cited once, bracketed with two other works in a sentence about repeated attempts at Python frontends for numerics-intensive programs. Nothing is run.

entries.name: OpenCilk: A Modular and Extensible Software Infrastructure for Fast Task-Parallel Code
entries.summary: An open-source task-parallel platform built around Tapir/LLVM, designed so that its compiler, runtime and tools can each be modified independently by researchers. Seq appears in the survey of work built on Tapir/LLVM, recorded there as compiling and running parallel tasks on a custom OpenMP back end.
entries.why_codon: The related-work section states that Shajii et al. introduce the Seq language for bioinformatics, which uses Tapir/LLVM to compile and run parallel tasks on a custom OpenMP back end. Nothing here builds on or runs Seq.
entries.note: The only citation in the corpus that runs the other way along the lineage. Everywhere else a work cites Codon or Seq as something it might use; here Seq is named as a downstream consumer of the citing paper's own infrastructure. Worth holding alongside the parallelism findings from the repository half, where no `implementation` entry touches Codon's GPU support.

entries.name: A Federated Learning Algorithms Development Paradigm
entries.summary: A development paradigm for federated learning algorithms built around PTB-FLA, a Python testbed aimed at edge and bare-metal deployment. Codon appears in the discussion of system performance, and the authors single out its bidirectional intermediate representation and SSA-form LLVM output as the property that would let them build a translator from compiled code into a behavioural model.
entries.why_codon: The paper devotes a paragraph to Codon as work highly related to system performance, describing it as a full language compiling Pythonic syntax to native code, and states that its bidirectional IR and SSA-form output make it interesting for the authors' project. No Codon code is written or run.
entries.note: Further evidence for the split running through this corpus: the paper opens on performance and then settles on the intermediate representation as the thing it actually wants. The Codon paper leads with speed; readers who plan to build something reach past it for the IR.

entries.name: Fast characterization of segmental duplication structure in multiple genome assemblies
entries.summary: BISER detects segmental duplications across several genome assemblies at homology levels where earlier tools break down, by decomposing the error between paralogs into a random point-mutation component and a clustered block-edit component and filtering on a Jaccard bound derived from the first. It reports the human genome in seven minutes on eight cores against SEDEF's hour and a quarter. The tool is written in Seq, which is what puts it in this index.
entries.why_codon: The paper states BISER is a framework implemented in the Seq programming language, citing both Seq papers at that point. Seq is the implementation language, not a subject of the work, and nothing about Seq itself is changed.
entries.note: Second paper-to-repository join, after secure-mice. Unlike that one the paper does not upgrade the repository's reading: 0xTCG/biser was already recorded as Seq source and the paper says the same. Worth noting that this is a Numanagic-lab paper, so the author-name scan matches its own byline and its self-citations to SEDEF; the Seq citation is reference 24, not the reference 22 the extractor also surfaced.

entries.name: mapquik: Efficient low-divergence mapping of long reads in minimizer space
entries.summary: A long-read mapper that chains multiple matched minimizers rather than single seeds, reporting order-of-magnitude speedups on HiFi reads. Seq is cited for a specific published result: the two orders of magnitude it achieved on the homology table reconstruction of the CORA read mapper.
entries.why_codon: The paper states that the domain-specific language Seq was developed to speed up genomic sequence analysis and achieved two orders of magnitude improvement in CORA's homology table reconstruction. The figure is quoted from the Seq paper; Seq is not used here.
entries.note: One of the few citations in the corpus that carries a number across. Most works cite the Codon family for what it is; this one cites it for what it measured.

entries.name: Design of a New Language Seeks Literature Survey
entries.venue: International Journal for Research in Applied Science and Engineering Technology
entries.summary: A literature survey of language and compiler projects aimed at making high-level code run fast, walking through each in turn and stating what it contributes. Seq is summarised in that sequence, described as a domain-specific language for computational biology, alongside Numba, the Wolfram Language compiler and a Python-to-FPGA prototype.
entries.why_codon: The survey names the Seq paper and its authors and summarises its contribution in a short numbered list. It reads published work and runs none of it.
entries.note: Second work filed as `survey`. It sets Seq among general-purpose Python accelerators rather than among bioinformatics tools, which is the framing the repository half found in the coursework and benchmark lanes rather than in the Numanagic lane.

entries.name: Taming the Zoo: The Unified GraphIt Compiler Framework for Novel Architectures
entries.summary: A unified compiler framework letting one graph DSL target CPUs, GPUs and novel graph accelerators from a single algorithm specification. Seq is one of several citations behind the observation that domain-specific languages have been used to abstract hardware across domains, standing in for bioinformatics in a list that also names machine learning, image processing, networking and tensor algebra.
entries.why_codon: Seq is cited once, as the bioinformatics entry in a bracketed list of domains where DSLs abstract hardware. No experiment involves it.
entries.note: One of three works in this batch from the same research group as the anchors, alongside D2X and OpenCilk. All three cite Seq the same way -- as an established example of the DSL argument rather than as a tool they use.

entries.name: Minimizer-space de Bruijn graphs: Whole-genome assembly of long reads in minutes on a personal computer
entries.summary: De Bruijn graphs built over minimizers rather than bases, which assembles a human genome from HiFi reads in minutes on a personal computer where k-mer counting alone took a day. The Seq preprint is cited once, as one of two exemplars of read mapping in the opening survey of sequence-analysis advances.
entries.why_codon: The single inline citation places the Seq preprint in a bracketed pair given as examples of read mapping. Neither Seq nor Codon is named anywhere in the body, and neither is used.
entries.note: Read from the bioRxiv preprint, 10.1101/2021.06.09.447586, which the harvest holds as a separate candidate; the Cell Systems record is used as the entry because it is the published version. That pair is a preprint and its own published form rather than two works, unlike the Sequre and Shechi pair that ruling 4 kept separate, so they are collapsed here. Worth his confirmation that collapsing is right, and worth checking whether other preprint-and-published pairs are sitting in the candidate list unnoticed.
